        DELAWARE BASIN MIDSTREAM LLC’S EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR
                              DECISION


         Delaware Basin Midstream LLC (“DBM”) files its Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision
(the “PFD”).1 The deadline to file exceptions to the PFD is September 2, 2026.2 Therefore, this
filing is timely made. In support, DBM respectfully shows as follows:

                                                 SUMMARY

         DBM excepts to the PFD’s conclusions that Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and
LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, the “Applicants”) failed to demonstrate
that the proposed transmission lines in Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475, which make up Import Path
2, are not “necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public” and do
not satisfy the need for additional service.3 The PFD explicitly contradicts the policies and
decisions of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”), as confirmed in two other
765-kV transmission line matters, Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315. Further, the ALJs improperly
substituted their own judgment for the Commission’s by rejecting the S&P Global Study on which
the Commission relied upon to approve the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”), and
improperly imposed a “partial build study” requirement. DBM asks the Commission to correct the
identified portions of the PFD, reject the recommendation to deny the Application, and find that
Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public
under PURA § 37.056(a).
                                                DISCUSSION

  I.     Introduction

         DBM proposes no exceptions to this section.

VII.    Need (Issues 5-7)

    a. The PFD is Contrary to the Findings of Need in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315.

        The Commission may only grant a certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) if the
Commission finds it “is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public.”4 The PFD wrongly denies the Application, finding that it is not necessary under § 37.056
due to post-PBRP developments concerning the load forecasts supporting Import Path 2’s need.5
This conclusion is contrary to the findings of need made in companion PBRP dockets and must be
rejected.
        The Commission faced the identical post-PBRP developments in Docket Nos. 59029 and
59315. Contrary to the PFD, the Commission found that § 37.056(a) need was established in both
cases.6 Specifically, in relevant part, the August 28, 2026 Order in Docket No. 59315 established
the following:

         The ALJs’ departure from the approach outlined in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 creates
regulatory uncertainty across the entire PBRP program. As plainly stated by the PUC on its
website, “[t]he PBRP is the first in a series of regional reliability plans . . . to ensure grid reliability

    b. The PFD infringes on the discretion afforded to the Commission.

        “Administrative agencies possess by implication such powers as may be necessary to
effectuate the legislative objectives which underlie the administrative powers expressly conferred
upon them.”14 In fact, the Commission “has been given more control than some other agencies
over the ultimate disposition of its cases.”15
        The ALJs’ need finding should be rejected because it substitutes the ALJs’ own judgment
for a discretionary Commission decision that has never been revisited or rescinded. Specifically,
the ALJs infringed on the Commission’s discretion by rejecting the S&P Global Study. As stated
above, under § 2003.049(g)(1)(A), the Commission has authority to change an ALJ’s finding or
conclusion where the ALJ “did not properly apply or interpret applicable law, commission rules
or policies, or prior administrative decisions.”16
        In the PFD’s rejection of the PBRP, the ALJs rely heavily on their disregard of the S&P
Global Study, which is the 2022 load forecast that ERCOT used as the basis for the oil and gas
load projections in the PBRP. But the Commission itself relied on that same study when it
approved the PBRP in October 2024 and reaffirmed the 765-kV import paths in April 2025.17 As
aptly put by the Third Court of Appeals:
                    [b]ecause administrative agencies are given their statutory powers with a view to
                    achieving legislative purposes more fully and effectively through the agency’s
                    specialized judgment, knowledge, and experience, the methods chosen by the

                     agency, and its interpretation of the statute it is required to administer, are entitled
                    to judicial respect.18
        When the Commission approved the PBRP and relied on the S&P Global Study to do so,
it was exercising precisely this kind of specialized agency judgment in furtherance of the Texas
legislature’s directive to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin.19 Specifically, the
Commission found that 765-kV transmission lines “will increase access to available generation
capacity to meet the region’s growing electricity needs[,]” as outlined in the S&P Global Study.20
        Notably, the PFD cites to Senate Bill 6, relating to interconnection of large electrical loads,
to further undermine the PBRP.21 This is yet another area where the PFD oversteps its bounds; it
is up the Commission to determine the impact of SB 6 on the PBRP, not a SOAH ALJ. As of this
filing, the Commission has not rescinded the PBRP. Thus, the PBRP and its reliance on the S&P
Global Study are both current Commission policy that the ALJs are required to abide by in issuing
the PFD. The recent orders in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 confirm that position. By rejecting
the study that the Commission relied upon to approve the PBRP, the ALJs failed to apply prior
Commission policy and decisions. If the PBRP is to be reconsidered, that is a decision for the
Commission, not the ALJs.
        Moreover, if there were issues that the ALJs thought cast doubt on the reliability of the
PBRP, including revisions to load forecasts, then the proper avenue to address those issues is
through certifying a question. Commission rules permit an ALJ to certify to the Commission issues
of “whether [C]ommission policy should be . . . clarified as to a substantive or procedural issue of
significance to the proceeding.”22 Certification to the Commission of whether updates to the
applicable load forecasts impact the Commission’s position on utilization of 765-kV transmission

        As the PBRP and its reliance on the S&P Global Study still stands, the ALJs have infringed
upon the Commission’s discretion. Therefore, DBM excepts to the following portions of the PFD,
which should be changed pursuant to § 2003.049(g):

    c. The PFD improperly requires a project specific study not required by PURA or
       Commission Rules.

        The PFD denies the Application in part because Applicants did not perform a “partial build
study” isolating Import Path 2’s need from the other two 765-kV import paths.23 PURA § 37.056
and 16 TAC § 25.101 set the need standard for CCN applications. Those provisions require the
Commission to consider things like the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional
service, and other enumerated factors.24 A partial build analysis is not among them. The
Commission approved the PBRP without one, and that was the Commission’s decision to make.
        Further, the authority to require transmission planning studies belongs to the Commission,
not SOAH. ERCOT has comprehensive authority over bulk transmission planning under 16 TAC
§ 25.361(d), and the Commission retains authority to recommend or direct transmission
construction under 16 TAC § 25.101(h). This authority does not extend to an ALJ.
        The PFD acknowledges that Applicants present the three 765-kV import paths as a single
comprehensive reliability solution.25 Yet, the PFD determines that Applicants should have
demonstrated independent need for Import Path 2.26 Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 have already
established the Commission’s position: the import paths that comprise the PBRP are each

 deny the Application, (3) find that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation,
 convenience, or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056(a), and (4) grant DBM such other and
 further relief to which it may be entitled.

    c. The PFD improperly requires a project specific study not required by PURA or
       Commission Rules.

         The PFD denies the Application in part because Applicants did not perform a "partial build
study" isolating Import Path 2's need from the other two 765-kV import paths.23 PURA § 37.056
and 16 TAC § 25.101 set the need standard for CCN applications. Those provisions require the
Commission to consider things like the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional
service, and other enumerated factors.24 A partial build analysis is not among them. The
Commission approved the PBRP without one, and that was the Commission's decision to make.
         Further, the authority to require transmission planning studies belongs to the Commission,
not SOAH. ERCOT has comprehensive authority over bulk transmission planning under 16 TAC
§ 25.361(d), and the Commission retains authority to recommend or direct transmission
construction under 16 TAC § 25.101(h). This authority does not extend to an ALJ.
         The PFD acknowledges that Applicants present the three 765-kV import paths as a single
comprehensive reliability solution.25 Yet, the PFD determines that Applicants should have
demonstrated independent need for Import Path 2.26 Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 have already
established the Commission' s position: the import paths that comprise the PBRP are each
